opus-5.5.text:
I think people often frame scaling and sample efficiency as opposites, as if you either throw more data at the problem or get cleverer about using less. In formal mathematics, I see them as complementary, almost necessarily so.

Start with the scarcity. Compared with natural language or code, there's very little formal math out there. Mathlib is a remarkable community achievement, but it's tiny next to the internet. If you want models that reason rigorously, which means every step checkable in something like Lean, you don't have an internet's worth of verified proofs to train on. So when we talk about building an internet-scale dataset, we're really talking about manufacturing one. We use autoformalization, synthetic problem generation, and having the system attempt proofs, fail, and try again.

That's where sample efficiency comes in. Each sample in formal math carries an unusually strong signal, because the proof checker gives you ground truth. A proof is either verified or it isn't. There's no fuzzy reward model and no human rater who might be tired that day. So every attempt, including the failed ones, tells you something precise, like "this tactic broke at this step." That makes each example far more informative than, say, a random paragraph scraped from the web.

So the way I think about it is that verification lets you scale without drowning in noise. In other domains, synthetic data at scale risks model collapse, where you're training on your own hallucinations. With a verifier in the loop, you can generate enormous amounts of data and keep only what's correct. Scaling gets you coverage and diversity. Sample efficiency gets you a high signal from every example, and the checker keeps the whole thing honest.

There's a deeper point too. Mathematicians themselves are extraordinarily sample efficient. A great mathematician might read a few key papers and develop an intuition that carries them through a whole career. We're not there with machines yet. But I think the path runs through scale first. You build a rich enough corpus of verified reasoning that the model starts internalizing structure, meaning which abstractions are useful and which lemmas tend to unlock things. Then that structure is what makes learning from new examples more efficient. Scale buys you the priors, and good priors buy you efficiency.

So the dataset isn't the end goal. It's the substrate for a self-improving loop, where the model proposes, the verifier checks, and the verified results feed back in. If that loop works, scale and efficiency stop being a trade-off and start compounding.

r001.rationale: The candidate says scale and efficiency “start compounding,” explaining that scale builds useful priors and those priors make learning more efficient. This communicates a multiplicative relationship.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that scaling and sample efficiency are not opposites, they're two sides of a tradeoff you keep renegotiating as the data changes.

When we started building out a large-scale mathematics dataset, the naive assumption was that more is always better. Just scrape everything, every arXiv paper, every textbook, every forum thread, and let the model sort it out. And at the beginning that's roughly true. When you're data-poor, the marginal value of one more example is very high, so breadth matters more than selection.

But mathematics is different from general web text in one important way. Most of it is wrong, or incomplete, or written at a level of informality where a human can fill in the gaps but a model can't tell whether a step is justified or just asserted. So as you scale, you very quickly hit a regime where the extra data is mostly noise with the same structure as signal. That's where sample efficiency becomes the real constraint. A million unverified proof sketches might teach the model less than ten thousand proofs that have been formally checked, because the checked ones give you a clean gradient and the rest give you a confident model that's confidently wrong.

So the way I think about it now is that scale buys you coverage, and verification buys you efficiency. Our job is to find the point where those cross. In practice that means we spend a lot of effort on the generation side, getting humans and systems to produce candidates at scale, and then an equal amount on the filtering side, using formal tools like Lean to decide what actually survives. The verifier is what lets you be aggressive about scale without drowning in it.

One more thing I'd add is that the relationship isn't static. Every time the model gets better, it changes what counts as an efficient sample. Problems that were informative last year are trivial now, so the dataset has to move with the frontier. That's why I think of it less as building a dataset and more as building a pipeline that keeps generating the right data for where the model is today.

r001.rationale: The response describes scaling and sample efficiency as a tradeoff: scale provides coverage, while verification improves efficiency. It does not characterize their relationship as multiplicative.

astra-6.text:
I think scaling and sample efficiency are complementary. Scaling asks how much more capability we can get from more data and compute. Sample efficiency asks how much we can learn from each example. When you’re building an internet-scale dataset, you have to care about both, because more data doesn’t necessarily mean more useful information.

You could add millions of examples that repeat what the model already knows, or you could add a much smaller set that covers something it hasn’t seen. So the question is not just, “How big is the dataset?” It’s also, “What does each additional example contribute?” That makes diversity, quality, and redundancy important.

I’d want a feedback loop between the dataset and the model: scale the data, understand where learning improves and where it stalls, and use that to guide what you collect next. Better sample efficiency makes scaling more productive, and scaling lets you explore a broader range of examples.

r001.rationale: The response calls scaling and sample efficiency complementary and says each helps the other, but it does not characterize their relationship as multiplicative.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scaling and sample efficiency are complementary. Scaling gives you more coverage, but sample efficiency asks how much useful learning you get from each example. For an internet-scale dataset, the goal shouldn’t simply be to collect as much data as possible. It should be to make additional data contribute something—whether that’s a new concept, a different context, or a case the model currently struggles with.

So I’d think about this as a feedback loop: scale the dataset, understand where the model improves and where it still fails, and use that to guide what you collect next. If you keep adding redundant examples, the dataset gets larger without necessarily becoming much more useful. Better selection can make scaling more effective, and scaling can help you discover what better selection should look like.

r001.rationale: The response describes scaling and sample efficiency as complementary and mutually informative, but it does not characterize their relationship as multiplicative.
